query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix will overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.intervention: Introduction of a nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation
generation.conditions: Temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, varying load and environment
generation.mechanism: Multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates, releasing gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear
generation.predicted_outcome: Low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix without nanohierarchical architecture
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, load up to 9 N, and ambient environment
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of the nanohierarchical architecture in reducing friction and wear, and the optimal composition and structure of the architecture

falsification_experiment.design: Sliding wear experiment with a nanohierarchical architecture-introduced CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix and a baseline CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix, under varying temperature, load, and environment conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduced nanohierarchical architecture does not result in a significant reduction in coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the baseline material, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: AbstractSustained wear damages on the sliding surfaces of alloys are generally the culprit responsible for the failure of various mechanical systems. Inspired by high-entropy effects, here we deliberately deploy nanohierarchical architecture with composition undulation in a Ni50(AlNbTiV)50 complex concentrated alloy, which yields ultralow wear rate within the order of 10−7 to 10−6 mm3/Nm between room temperature and 800 °C. Such remarkable wear resistance heretofore represents one of the highest wear resistance reported for the bulk alloys or composites, and originates from the multi-type adaptive friction interface protection governed by intrinsically nano-coupled grains and nanoprecipitates. This cooperative heterostructure releases gradient frictional stress in stages upon wear at room temperature through the coexistence of multiple deformation pathways while activating a dense nanocrystalline glaze layer upon wear at 800 °C to minimize adhesive and oxidative wear. Our work uncovers a practical avenue for tailoring wear properties with multicomponent heterostructures over a wide temperature range.

cited_evidence.text: Figure 3A shows the Vickers hardness and wear rate variations of NiX and Ni3X as the temperature increases from RT to 800 °C. The hardness of NiX and Ni3X gradually decreases from 6.1 GPa and 4.3 GPa at RT to 3.7 GPa and 2.5 GPa at 800 °C, respectively. The high thermal hardness of NiX arises from the solid solution strengthening and the resultant heterostructures [,]. The trend in wear rate of the Ni3X with temperature is similar to that of the conventional alloys. Specifically, its wear rate increases from 1.1 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at RT to 4.2 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 600 °C, but decreases afterward to 2.4 × 10−5 mm3/Nm at 800 °C. However, the wear rate of the NiX is basically maintained at the order of (10−7 to 10−6) mm3/Nm over the entire test temperature. In particular, it achieves ultra-low wear at RT (1.7 × 10−7 mm3/Nm) and 800 °C (9.1 × 10−7 mm3/Nm).
